newsitem.title: GERMANY: German broadcasters want more explicit sex on TV.
newsitem.headline: German broadcasters want more explicit sex on TV.

text.p: German broadcasters, who already show enough nudity to make more prudish nationalities blush, demanded on Wednesday a change in the law to allow them to show even more explicit sex on television.

"The law urgently needs to be liberalised and brought up to date. We need to be a part of the new media landscape," Andreas Vrede, the programme director of Premiere television told a meeting of politicians, academics and journalists.

Premiere, Germany's largest pay television channel, and two new channels applying for licences in Germany want to broadcast films showing "real sex" after midnight. These films could only be seen using a decoder to prevent children from watching them.
They want to air films that show the full sexual act and sexual organs -- rather than just suggesting them.

A recent survey for Die Woche weekly paper showed that more than 50 percent of Germans, renowned for their relaxed attitude towards pornography, said they were in favour of this and the appropriate change in current legislation.

Sex has become a staple part of the television diet in Germany in the last few years as 30 channels on the cable network battle for viewers in what has become Europe's most lucrative television market.

The market has been swamped with sex-talk shows, reportage on prostitution, strippers and unusual sexual practices as well as low-budget "soft-porn" films featuring leather-trousered men chasing bare-breasted barmaids.

Although much of this steamy material would be slammed as "pornography" in the Anglo-Saxon world, many Germans think their shows are tame compared with what is on offer in nearby Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.
Some academics and politicians agree the law should be changed as long as a strict ban is upheld on "harder pornography" such as violence or sex with children or animals.

Heribert Schumann, a professor of law at Leipzig University, argued that the current German legal definition of pornography was muddled and old-fashioned, and was based on a misguided belief that all pornography was harmful to children.
"Studies have shown that pornography does not necessarily have a harmful effect on young people and this must be reflected in the law," Schumann told the meeting.
Under a 1968 ruling, German law defines pornography as anything "designed to cause sexual stimulation", which "reduces characters to sex objects" and "shows sex organs in a coarse way."

Anything which can be labelled "pornographic" under this definition is illegal. But in practice broadcasters can show relatively explicit sex scenes after 11 p.m. as long as sexual organs and the full sexual act are not shown.

Horst Eylmann, the head of a German parliamentary committee on legal affairs, said changes in pornography laws were politically impossible. "I can't see the law being changed and I have not heard a better definition of pornography."
Germany, like much of Europe, reacted with horror over several paedophile murder cases in recent years, which sparked calls for tougher penalties for child-sex offenders.

"I don't think the law will be changed at the moment, because after all these cases involving children it is very difficult for politicians to take a stand in favour of more sex on television," said Premiere's Wrede.
Joerg Tauss, information and communications spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said the debate about television sex was being overtaken by technological advances.

"The biggest problem now is uncontrolled pornography on the Internet. Let German subscription television show more pornography after midnight. But we cannot regulate the World Wide Web by imposing time limits," Tauss told the meeting.

Germany wants legislation to keep pornography and Nazi propaganda off the Internet -- although many other countries believe the global system of computers linked by telephone lines is beyond regulation.
